PYPI PROVENANCE CHECK · TWO READ-ONLY REQUESTS PER PACKAGE

Which of your Python dependencies lack a provenance attestation?

Paste a requirements.txt, a PEP 621 pyproject.toml, or a plain list of package names, and see which ones were published with a PyPI provenance attestation -- PEP 740, PyPI's trusted-publishing signature (OIDC, no long-lived API token to steal) -- and which still rely on a classic upload token.

Your file is parsed in this browser and never uploaded. Checking a package makes two GET requests, from your browser, to the public PyPI API -- pypi.org's package metadata endpoint, then its PEP 740 integrity/provenance endpoint.

1. Paste a requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or a plain list

2. Provenance by package

PackageVersion checkedProvenanceDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this in CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

node cli.mjs requirements.txt
node cli.mjs requirements.txt --json
node cli.mjs requirements.txt --without-provenance-only
node cli.mjs pyproject.toml                     # unpinned deps: checks the latest published version
echo "pip\nsix==1.17.0" | node cli.mjs -         # freeform list on stdin

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. Reads only the file you name; the only network calls are the per-package PyPI lookups.

Common questions

Why isn't pypi-attestations verify enough?

pypi-attestations verify checks one already-downloaded artifact at a time, from the command line, with no bulk or CI-friendly report across a requirements file or several repositories. This tool works from a pasted requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or plain list -- no download or install required -- and the CLI emits JSON for scripting. More: why this exists alongside pypi-attestations.

Does a package without provenance mean it's compromised?

No. PyPI attestations only became available in November 2024, so most published packages predate the feature or their maintainer hasn't migrated yet -- popular, actively maintained packages show up with no provenance attestation too. And the reverse isn't a safety guarantee either: a documented May 2026 worm shipped malicious PyPI and npm packages carrying valid, verifiable attestations, because an attestation proves how a release was built, not that its source code is safe. The absence or presence of provenance is a fact about how a version was published, not a verdict on whether it is safe to install.

Is my requirements.txt uploaded anywhere?

No. The file is parsed entirely in your browser. What does leave your browser is two read-only GET requests per package name/version -- one to pypi.org's package metadata API, one to its PEP 740 integrity/provenance API -- the same public endpoints pip and pypi-attestations already talk to.

What counts as a provenance attestation?

PyPI's integrity API (PEP 740) serves a non-empty attestation_bundles array for a release file published via trusted publishing from a supported CI. This tool reports exactly that: present or absent, and, when present, the publisher's repository and workflow from the attestation's own certificate.

How is this different from a supply-chain security platform like Socket?

Different layers. Socket watches a connected dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis across dozens of risk categories, including Python. This tool answers one narrower, one-time question from a pasted requirements file or the CLI: does this exact release file carry PyPI's own PEP 740 provenance attestation? See this checker vs. Socket.

Been checking packages one at a time on pypi.org? See this checker vs. checking each package on PyPI by hand.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not security advice, and it does not replace a qualified security review. It reports one factual field the PyPI integrity API publishes about each release file you asked about -- nothing more. The absence of a provenance attestation is not evidence of compromise, and its presence is not a guarantee of safety. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The file you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Checking a package sends its name and version to the public PyPI API, from your browser, over HTTPS -- nothing about your project beyond what you pasted. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over the same dependency tree: npm Provenance Check is the same idea for JavaScript's registry, and Dependency Confusion Check flags a pip --extra-index-url or unscoped npm setup that lets an attacker's package win over your private one.

vs-checking-each-package-on-pypi-by-hand.text:
← PyPI Provenance Check

PyPI Provenance Check vs. checking each package on PyPI by hand

Opening one package's PyPI page and checking its provenance information works fine for a single dependency you're curious about. It does not scale to a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml with dozens of packages, each needing the right pinned version's page found among however many releases that project has, checked, and the result written down — which is what this free, no-upload checker does in one pass from a pasted file.

Where checking it yourself stops being enough

Anyone curious about one specific dependency already does this: open its page on pypi.org, find the release you actually installed, and look for provenance information. For a single package that's a minute of clicking. The problem is a real dependency set is rarely one package — it's a requirements file with dozens of direct and transitive entries, and the manual version of this check does not get easier per-package as the list grows.

What you're trying to confirmChecking pypi.org yourselfThis checker
Whether one specific package's page shows provenance information.Works. This is the one case a single manual lookup reliably handles.Also handles it, in the same pass as every other package in your file.
Finding the exact release that matches your pin — ==, >=, a range, or no pin at all (meaning whatever resolves latest) — among however many releases that project has published.Requires remembering which pin syntax means what while clicking through a project's release history, for every package.Resolved against PyPI's own metadata API the same way every time, for every package in the file.
Doing the same lookup consistently across a requirements file with dozens of direct and transitive dependencies.The same several clicks repeated dozens of times, with no running tally except what you remember or type into a separate note; easy to drop a row partway through.Every package in the pasted file, checked the same mechanical way, with nothing skipped.
Producing a list of just the packages still missing an attestation, in a form you can hand to a teammate or feed to a migration tracker.Nothing beyond whatever you wrote down yourself while clicking through pages.The CLI emits exactly that list as JSON in one run.
Re-checking the whole dependency set again after a requirements file changes.The full manual pass again, one package at a time.One paste, the whole file, every time.

A quick look at one package's page is still the fastest way to answer a one-off question, and this checker isn't reading anything pypi.org doesn't already publish — it's reading the same PEP 740 integrity API a manual check would eventually reach, just resolving every package in a pasted file automatically instead of leaving the lookup to be repeated by hand across however many dependencies the file has.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: your file is parsed entirely in your browser, and only package names and versions ever leave it, in read-only requests to PyPI's own public API.

Common questions

Can't I just look up each package on pypi.org myself?

For one package, yes -- open its PyPI page, find the release you actually installed, and check its provenance information. What doesn't scale is doing that for every package in a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml: each one needs its own page found, the specific pinned (or latest) version's release located among however many releases that project has published, and the result written down somewhere before you move to the next package. This tool resolves and checks every package in a pasted file in one pass.

Why is matching the right release version easy to get wrong by hand?

A requirements.txt pins versions in several different ways -- an exact ==, a floor >=, a range, or no pin at all (meaning whatever resolves as latest at install time) -- and a popular package can have dozens or hundreds of published releases. Finding the one release page that matches what your pin actually resolves to, for every package in the file, is the kind of lookup that is reliable when a tool does it the same way every time and error-prone when it depends on remembering which pin syntax means what while clicking through release history.

Why is it easy to lose track partway through a long dependency list?

A typical project's requirements file runs to dozens of direct and transitive dependencies. Checking each one by hand means repeating the same several clicks -- find the package, find the right release, look for provenance information, note the result -- dozens of times in a row, with no running tally except what you remember or type into a separate note. It is the same kind of repetitive, easy-to-drop-a-row task a mechanical pass through a pasted file does exactly the same way every time.

What do I get from a manual check that this tool doesn't produce?

Nothing extra -- both read the same PyPI facts. What a manual pass through pypi.org doesn't produce on its own is a single list of which packages in your file lack an attestation, in a form you can hand to a teammate, paste into a migration tracker, or feed to another script. This tool's CLI emits that list as JSON in one run; a manual check produces only whatever you wrote down yourself.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit any maintainer or reviewer already has -- opening a package's PyPI page and checking its provenance information before trusting it. It names no competing product or company. This tool makes only read-only requests to PyPI's own public API, the same facts a manual page visit would show.

Already know about PyPA's own verification tool? Read why not just pypi-attestations verify.

This checker vs. Socket

Two different layers: Socket watches a connected dependency graph and the public registries -- including PyPI -- on an ongoing basis across 70+ risk categories. This tool answers one narrower, one-time question from a pasted requirements.txt or the CLI — does this exact release file carry a PEP 740 provenance attestation — with no account and nothing installed.

What each product is for

Socket is a supply-chain security platform. Its own site describes deep package inspection that characterizes what a dependency actually does, connected through a GitHub app, a CLI (Socket publishes its own security CLI on PyPI, confirming Python coverage), or a browser extension, and it flags more than 70 categories of risk across PyPI, npm, and other ecosystems — malware, typosquatting, hidden or obfuscated code, and permission creep among them — while monitoring a project's dependency graph on an ongoing basis. It is free for public, open-source use, and Socket's own site lists paid tiers for private-repository and organization use. This page does not claim to know exactly how Socket weighs or surfaces PEP 740 provenance specifically, since this session cannot verify that live against Socket's own product.

This tool does none of what Socket does. It has no account, no ongoing service, no GitHub app, and it never scores a package or a project. Given a pasted requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, or a plain list of package names, it makes two read-only GET requests per package to pypi.org — the same public API pip and pypi-attestations already talk to — and reports exactly whether a PEP 740 provenance attestation exists for the resolved release file: present (published via trusted publishing from a supported CI) or absent (a classic, stealable API token). Nothing is uploaded, nothing is connected, and nothing is remembered between runs beyond what you paste again next time.

QuestionWhere to answer it

I want a GitHub app or CLI that watches every future pull request for newly introduced supply-chain risk.Socket — this tool has no memory between runs and watches nothing on its own.
I want a single, exportable report across several projects' requirements files with no sign-up, wired into a script with --json.This tool's CLI — paste or point it at each requirements file in turn.
I want to know whether a specific package has ever shown malicious behavior, or is a typosquat of a popular name.Socket — this tool checks one attestation field and cannot answer that.
I want the exact PEP 740 attestation field, per release file, with no interpretation or score layered on top.This tool — that is the one fact it reports, nothing more.

A team can reasonably run both: Socket for continuous, registry-aware defense against a live attack already under way, and this tool as a fast, zero-account, zero-install check of exactly which dependencies still publish through a stealable token — useful on its own, or before deciding whether Socket's broader connected monitoring is worth setting up at all. This page does not evaluate Socket's detection accuracy or how it weighs provenance and makes no claim about either — it only describes Socket's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. A clean result from either one is not a guarantee that a dependency is safe: absence of a provenance attestation is a fact about how a release was published, not a verdict, and presence is not a safety guarantee either -- a May 2026 worm shipped malicious PyPI and npm packages carrying valid, verifiable attestations.

why-not-just-pypi-attestations-verify.ht.text:
← back to PyPI Provenance Check

Why not just pypi-attestations verify?

PyPA's own tool already verifies a PEP 740 attestation:

pip install pypi-attestations
pypi-attestations verify pypi --repository https://pypi.org

It's the reference implementation, it's accurate, and if all you want is a one-time answer for one artifact you already have, it's the right tool -- this page isn't arguing against it. What it doesn't do is what this tool exists for.

Three gaps this tool fills

1. It needs one artifact at a time, already resolved. pypi-attestations verify checks a single wheel or sdist you point it at -- a URL or a local path. This tool works from a pasted requirements.txt, PEP 621 pyproject.toml, or even a plain list of names, resolving each package's latest or pinned version and its file itself. Useful when you're evaluating a whole dependency set before installing it, reviewing someone else's requirements file they sent you, or checking a repo you haven't cloned.

2. It's one package at a time, with no report to hand off. If you maintain (or audit) more than one project, there's no built-in way to see "which of these 40 repos still has unmigrated dependencies" without invoking the CLI once per artifact and collecting results by hand. This tool's CLI emits --json for the whole file in one run, so a script can loop over repos and diff the output.

3. No bulk or CI-shaped output. pypi-attestations verify is built to verify one artifact's cryptographic bundle, not to summarize a project's dependency tree. The CLI here has a flag built for exactly that:

node cli.mjs requirements.txt --without-provenance-only --json

which returns just the packages still missing an attestation, as JSON, ready to file into a spreadsheet, a Slack digest, or a migration tracker.

What both tools read is the same fact

There is no separate provenance database. Both pypi-attestations verify and this tool read from PyPI's PEP 740 integrity API -- attestation_bundles on a release file -- so they will never disagree about whether a given file carries an attestation. The difference is entirely in what you can start from and what you get out, not in what's being measured. pypi-attestations verify additionally checks the attestation's cryptographic validity end-to-end (the Sigstore bundle, the certificate chain, the Trusted Publisher identity match); this tool reports presence/absence and the publisher named in the certificate, but does not itself re-verify the cryptographic signature -- for that, run pypi-attestations verify against the specific file this tool flags.

Common questions

Does pypi-attestations verify already do this?

It verifies the same underlying attestation this tool reports on, and it does the full cryptographic check this tool does not. What it does not do is work from a requirements file or pyproject.toml before you have downloaded anything, produce a report across more than one project, or emit JSON another tool can consume in bulk. Those three gaps are what this tool adds.

Do pypi-attestations verify and this tool ever disagree about presence/absence?

No. Both read from PyPI's own PEP 740 integrity API for the exact same release file. There is no separate provenance database for either tool to disagree about.

When should I use pypi-attestations verify instead?

When you already have a specific artifact (a URL or a downloaded file) and need the full cryptographic verification -- certificate chain, Sigstore bundle, Trusted Publisher identity match -- not just a presence/absence report across a dependency list.
